Subject: SNAT implications for PrivateLink vs Peering vs S2S — pilot context

Kim and team,

Thanks again for the walkthrough last week. As we prepare the pilot we hit a sticky operational question from our networking team: how does SNAT interact with Redwood Private when we use PrivateLink (interface endpoints) compared to VPC peering or a site-to-site VPN? Our primary concerns:

- Source IP preservation for upstream IDS/IPS and rate-limiting rules
- Auditability (can we see real tenant IPs in logs)
- NAT traversal complexity for mutual TLS + client certs

We attached our high-level network diagram and a short test-plan draft. Can Redwood confirm expected behavior in each mode and any operational mitigations you recommend (e.g., proxy sidecar, preserving X-Forwarded-For, or using a transit appliance)? Also curious about any SLA/latency differences you typically see for PrivateLink vs peering vs S2S in Private deployments.

Appreciate an operational summary we can circulate to our security reviewers.

—Luke
EdgeCorp Platform

Attachments: edgecorp_network_diagram_v2.pdf (diagram), privatelink-snat-test-plan.xlsx (test cases)

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>

Cc: Connor Obrien <connor_obrien@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: SNAT implications for PrivateLink vs Peering vs S2S — pilot context

Hi Luke — thanks for the clear summary and the diagram. Putting a short operational note below; Connor and Ben are looped for technical validation and runbook items. I'll follow up with a one-page summary for your security team.

Quick answers up front:
- VPC Peering: preserves source IPs end-to-end, so your upstream IDS will see client IPs. Simpler for mutual-TLS but requires route table coordination and does not scale well across many VPCs.
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): your traffic terminates on an ENI in our service VPC. By default the source IP seen in the Redwood dataplane will be the ENI (SNAT), so upstream logs will not show the original client IP unless we pass X-Forwarded-For or we run a proxy that forwards the original IP. It’s the more controlled surface for cross-account exposure and often preferred for compliance but requires explicit handling for source-IP needs.
- Site-to-site VPN: preserves source IPs inside the tunnel; behavior depends on your on-prem NAT policies. VPNs add complexity for scaling and you should validate MTU/path-MTU for large inference payloads.

Recommended mitigations depending on priority:
1) If source IPs are required in logs: enable header propagation (X-Forwarded-For) at the ingress proxy and ensure your IDS reads that header; or request a short-lived proxy sidecar in the Private deployment that preserves client IPs to downstream services.
2) For strong mutual-TLS and client-cert validation, peering or VPN are simpler for direct IP-based policy enforcement. PrivateLink still supports mTLS at the application layer but you lose IP-based client identity unless you propagate it.
3) If you need regional redundancy + minimal operational overhead, PrivateLink + a small NAT-aware proxy is a pragmatic middle ground.

Connor / Ben — can you validate the SNAT specifics, any current product flags for header propagation, and give an estimated latency delta we should present to EdgeCorp?

Thanks,
Kim
Principal Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

From: Connor Obrien <connor_obrien@redwood.ai>
To: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>, Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
Date: Sun, 15 Aug 2027 12:18:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: SNAT implications for PrivateLink vs Peering vs S2S — pilot context

Kim / Ben — technical validation below, copied into the thread for Luke.

Peering:
- Behavior: no SNAT within AWS VPC peering; packets keep client source IP. Good for IDS and IP allowlists.
- Tradeoffs: requires cross-account route table entries and security group tweaks. L4 ACLs work as expected. Scale: fine for a small set of peers but operationally heavy for 20+ accounts.
- Latency: baseline (measured on similar pilots) ~1–3 ms extra inside region vs PrivateLink; depends on backbone.

PrivateLink (Interface Endpoint):
- Behavior: traffic terminates at an ENI in the service VPC. The service typically sees the ENI IP as the source unless the service proxy reconstructs the original source header. Redwood's private runtime supports X-Forwarded-For propagation — there is a config toggle on the gateway.
- Tradeoffs: strong isolation, minimal route table changes, easier security posture but you must verify header acceptance across your stack. Also watch for flow logs showing ENI IP, which your security team may need to map.
- Latency: measured delta ~2–6 ms vs peering for requests with similar payload sizes and single-hop routing; slightly higher variance.

Site-to-site VPN:
- Behavior: tunnel preserves original source IP by default; depends on your on-prem NAT. Good for legacy IP-based policy engines.
- Tradeoffs: HA/throughput and path MTU issues; BGP session management if using dynamic routing. Also operationally heavier to manage and triage.

Operational notes:
- mTLS: all three models support mTLS; mutual TLS termination point matters. If termination happens at Redwood, client identity is available at application layer, not necessarily at network layer.
- Logs and correlation: we recommend a short mapping doc we can generate that maps ENI IPs to your tenant endpoints for a pilot window; that helps IDS correlation if you go PrivateLink.
- Test plan suggestion: run three short benchmarks (10k requests each) for functional (client IP visibility), latency P95, and end-to-end MTU test. Attachments look good; we can add a small SNAT-targeted test case.

I can draft the runbook steps and the command snippets (tcpdump, curl with --interface, checking X-Forwarded-For).

—Connor
Senior Infrastructure Engineer, Redwood Inference

Luke — attaching the short summary and an internal runbook we ran on a staging pilot. Top-line recommendation for your security reviewers:

- If your IDS requires source-IP visibility for immediate blocking decisions, choose VPC Peering (region-limited) or S2S VPN.
- If you prefer least-surface exposure and simpler cross-account controls, choose PrivateLink but add header propagation + a small proxy sidecar to preserve client IPs for logs/IDS.
- For the pilot, we recommend starting with PrivateLink + header propagation (lowest friction) and run the three SNAT-targeted tests. If the IDS blocking use-case fails your acceptance criteria, migrate to peering for that account.
